Drollery refers to a particular kind of humor — one that is quiet, dry, gently odd, and quietly amusing. It is the quality of being funny in a whimsical, understated, slightly peculiar way, without being loud, obvious, or trying too hard.

Think of it this way: if a clown slips on a banana peel, that is broad, physical comedy. If a sharp-tongued person delivers a biting insult disguised as a compliment, that is wit or sarcasm. But if someone says something oddly funny with a perfectly straight face — something a little eccentric, a little absurd, but never harsh — and you find yourself smiling quietly rather than laughing out loud, that is drollery at work.

The word "drollery" is used in two closely related ways:

1. As a quality or characteristic
When used this way, drollery refers to the general quality of being droll — the overall tone or atmosphere of quiet, whimsical humor that a person, a piece of writing, or a performance might have.

"His drollery made even the most boring meetings bearable."

Here, drollery describes a habitual quality the person has — a dry, gently amusing manner about them.

2. As a specific thing — a remark, story, or act
When used this way, a drollery (or "drolleries" in plural) refers to a specific instance of droll humor — a particular funny remark, a comic story, a jest, or an odd observation that quietly amuses people.

"She entertained the guests with her drolleries all evening."

Here, the drolleries are the individual funny things she said or did.
What Makes Drollery Distinct — What It Is and What It Is NOT

This is where the word gets really interesting, because drollery occupies a very specific territory in the world of humor. Understanding what it is not will sharpen your understanding of what it is.

Drollery is NOT slapstick.
Slapstick is loud, physical, and obvious — pratfalls, pies in faces, exaggerated reactions. Drollery is the opposite: subtle, understated, and cerebral in its quietness.

Drollery is NOT sharp wit.
Wit is clever, fast, and usually relies on intelligent wordplay or a brilliant turn of phrase. Drollery is softer and warmer than wit. It doesn't show off its intelligence. It is more gently odd than sharply clever.

Drollery is NOT sarcasm.
Sarcasm has an edge — it can sting. Drollery is almost never mean-spirited. It is good-natured and harmless.

Drollery is NOT boisterous comedy.
It doesn't make you roar with laughter. It makes you smile, perhaps chuckle softly, or even pause and think "wait — that's rather funny, isn't it?"

Drollery IS:

  • Quietly amusing
  • A little odd or whimsical
  • Often deadpan (delivered with a straight face, no winking at the audience)
  • Gentle and warm in spirit
  • Sometimes unintentionally funny — a person or situation can have an air of drollery without even trying to be funny
  • The kind of humor that grows on you rather than hitting you immediately
A Helpful Way to Picture It

Imagine a very composed, quietly eccentric old professor who, while lecturing about medieval history, says with complete seriousness: "The king's solution to the famine was to declare that hunger itself was illegal. Naturally, this solved nothing, but the paperwork was very thorough."

He doesn't smirk. He moves on immediately. But everyone in the room smiles. That is drollery — dry, odd, understated, gently absurd, and delivered without fanfare.
Drollery Can Describe People, Writing, and Situations

One useful thing to know is that this word can be applied in different contexts:

  • A person can be known for their drollery — meaning they have a dry, quietly funny personality.
  • A piece of writing (a novel, an essay, a speech) can be praised for its drollery — meaning it has a tone of gentle, whimsical humor woven through it.
  • A situation can have a certain drollery to it — meaning it is quietly, almost absurdly funny in the way it has unfolded, even if nobody planned for it to be.

In older English (particularly from the 1600s and 1700s), "drollery" also had some more specific meanings that you might encounter if you read older literature:

  • It could refer to a comic picture, caricature, or humorous illustration — a funny drawing.
  • It could refer to a short comic performance or puppet show, often performed at fairs and markets.
  • It could refer to a collection of comic stories, jests, or humorous tales published together in a book.

These older meanings all share the same DNA — something light, playful, and amusingly odd — but they refer to specific forms or products rather than the general quality of humor.

Drollery is the quality or expression of a gentle, dry, quietly whimsical kind of humor — the kind that makes you smile or chuckle softly rather than laugh loudly, and that never tries too hard or means any harm.
